'''''Areca catechu''''' is a species of [[Arecaceae|palm]] native to the [[Philippines]] cultivated for [[areca nut]]s.<ref name=GRIN/><ref name="Zumbroich2007">{{cite journal |last1=Zumbroich |first1=Thomas J. |title=The origin and diffusion of betel chewing: a synthesis of evidence from South Asia, Southeast Asia and beyond |journal=eJournal of Indian Medicine |date=2007–2008 |volume=1 |pages=87–140 |url=https://ugp.rug.nl/eJIM/article/download/24712/22162}}</ref><ref name="powo">{{cite web |title=''Areca catechu'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:664107-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew |access-date=2 May 2023}}</ref> It was carried widely through the tropics by the [[Austronesian expansion|Austronesian migrations]] and [[Spice trade|trade]] since at least 1500 BCE due to its use in [[betel nut chewing]].<ref name="Zumbroich2007"/> It is widespread in cultivation and is considered naturalized in much of tropical Asia and in [[Taiwan]], southern China ([[Guangxi]], [[Hainan]], [[Yunnan]]), [[Madagascar]], parts of the [[Pacific Islands]], and also in the [[West Indies]].<ref>Jones, D. (2001), ''Palms Throughout The World'', Reed New Holland, Australia.</ref><ref name = "Monograph" >

Its fruits (called [[areca nut]]s or betel nuts) are chewed together with [[Calcium hydroxide|slaked lime]] and betel leaves for their stimulant and narcotic effects.

==Taxonomy==
[[Image:Areca catechu - Köhler–s Medizinal-Pflanzen-014.jpg|thumb|left|19th century drawing of ''Areca catechu'']]
Common names in English include '''areca palm''', '''areca nut palm''', '''betel palm''', '''betel nut palm''', '''Indian nut''', '''Pinang palm''' and '''catechu'''.<ref name=GRIN/> This palm is commonly called the '''betel tree''' because its fruit, the [[areca nut]], which are often [[paan|chewed along]] with the [[Betel|betel leaf]], a leaf from a vine of the family [[Piperaceae]].

The species was first published by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his book ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' on page 1189 in 1753.<ref name="powo"/>

==Description==
[[File:Areca nut garden (1).jpg|220px|thumb|Areca nut garden]]
''Areca catechu'' is a medium-sized palm [[tree]], growing straight to {{convert|20|m|abbr=on}} tall, with a trunk {{convert|10–15|cm|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} in diameter. The [[leaf|leaves]] are {{convert|1.5–2|m|ft|abbr=on}} long, pinnate, with numerous, crowded leaflets.

==Chemical composition==
The seed contains [[alkaloid]]s such as [[arecaidine]] and [[arecoline]], which, when chewed, are intoxicating and slightly addictive. The seed also contains condensed [[tannins]] ([[procyanidins]]) called [[arecatannins]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=Screening of various plant extracts used in ayurvedic medicine for inhibitory effects on human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protease |first1=Ines Tomoco |last1=Kusumoto |first2=Takeshi |last2=Nakabayashi |first3=Hiroaki |last3=Kida |first4=Hirotsugu |last4=Miyashiro |first5=Masao |last5=Hattori |first6=Tsuneo |last6=Namba |first7=Kunitada |last7=Shimotohno |journal=Phytotherapy Research |volume=9 |issue=3 |year=1995 |pages=180–184 |doi=10.1002/ptr.2650090305 |s2cid=84577539 }}</ref> which are carcinogenic.

The [[antibacterial]] activity of the seed has been studied.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rama Bhat |first1=P. |last2=Savitri |first2=V.H. |last3=Laxmi |first3=P.G. |last4=Jenitta |first4=E.P. |title=A Study on the phytochemical analysis, silver nanoparticle synthesis and antibacterial activity from seed extract of ''Areca catechu'' L. |journal=International Journal of Biochemistry Research & Review |date=2016 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=1–9}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[Image:Areca farm.jpg|thumb|''Areca catechu'' farm in [[Kerala]], India]]

===Betel nut chewing===
{{Main|Betel nut chewing|Areca nut}}
''Areca catechu'' is grown for its commercially important seed crop, the [[areca nut]], which is the main component of the practice of [[betel nut chewing]]. It is popular throughout [[Southeast Asia]], [[South Asia]], [[Taiwan]], [[Papua New Guinea]], the [[Solomon Islands]], parts of southern [[China]], [[Madagascar]], and the [[Maldives]]. The nut itself can be addictive and has direct link to [[oral cancers]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Thomas and MacLennan|year=1992|title = Slaked lime and betel nut cancer in Papua New Guinea|journal=The Lancet|volume= 340|issue= 8819|pages= 577–578|doi= 10.1016/0140-6736(92)92109-S|pmid=1355157|s2cid=34296427}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author= Hemantha Amarasinghe|year= 2010|title= Betel-quid chewing with or without tobacco is a major risk factor for oral potentially malignant disorders in Sri Lanka: A case-control study|journal= Oral Oncology|volume= 46|issue= 4|pages= 297–301|doi= 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2010.01.017|pmid=20189448}}</ref> Chewing areca nut is a cause of [[oral submucous fibrosis]], a [[premalignant]] lesion which frequently progresses to [[mouth cancer]].<ref name=Ray2019>{{cite journal |vauthors=Ray JG, Chatterjee R, Chaudhuri K |title=Oral submucous fibrosis: A global challenge. Rising incidence, risk factors, management, and research priorities |journal=Periodontology 2000 |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=200–212 |date=2019 |pmid=31090137 |doi=10.1111/prd.12277 |s2cid=155089425 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Marcello Spinella|title=The psychopharmacology of herbal medicine: plant drugs that alter mind, brain, and behavior|url=https://archive.org/details/psychopharmacolo0000spin|url-access=registration|access-date=14 October 2011|year=2001|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-69265-6|pages=[https://archive.org/details/psychopharmacolo0000spin/page/233 233]–}}
</ref>

The practice of chewing [[areca nut]]s originated in [[Island Southeast Asia]], where the areca palm is native. The oldest known evidence of areca nut chewing was found in a burial pit in the [[Duyong Cave]] site in the [[Philippines]] (to which areca palms are native), which dates to around 4,630±250 [[Before Present|BP]]. Its diffusion is closely tied to the [[Neolithic]] expansion of the [[Austronesian peoples]]. It was spread to the Indo-Pacific during prehistoric times, reaching [[Micronesia]] at 3,500 to 3,000 BP, [[Near Oceania]] at 3,400 to 3,000 BP; [[South India]] and [[Sri Lanka]] by 3,500 BP; [[Mainland Southeast Asia]] by 3,000 to 2,500 BP; [[Northern India]] by 1500 BP; and [[Madagascar]] by 600 BP. From India, it was also spread westwards to [[Persia]] and the [[Mediterranean]]. It was also previously present in the [[Lapita culture]], based on archaeological remains dated from 3,600 to 2,500 BP, but it was not carried into [[Polynesia]].<ref name="Zumbroich2007"/>

===Other uses===
The areca palm is also used as an interior landscaping species. It is often used in large indoor areas such as malls and hotels. It will not fruit or reach full size if grown in this way. Indoors, it is a slow-growing, low-water, high-light plant that is sensitive to [[spider mite]]s and occasionally [[mealybug]]s.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

In India, the dried fallen leaves are collected and hot-pressed into [[disposable]] palm leaf plates and bowls.<ref>[http://www.thewholeleafco.com/page/1/compostable_palm_leaf_tableware/ Palm Leaf Plates] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160916165006/http://www.thewholeleafco.com/page/1/compostable_palm_leaf_tableware/ |date=2016-09-16 }} on the website TheWholeLeafCo.dom; viewed in September 2016</ref>

==Cultural significance==
[[File:Flag of Penang (Malaysia).svg|thumb|left|Areca nut on [[Penang]]'s flag]]
{{Main|Betel nut chewing}}
In Indonesia and Malaysia there are numerous place names using the words ''pinang'', ''jambi'' or ''jambe'' (areca in [[Javanese language|Javanese]], [[Sundanese language|Sundanese]], [[Balinese language|Balinese]], and [[Old Malay]]). For example, the cities of [[Tanjung Pinang]], [[Pangkal Pinang]] in Indonesia, the Indonesian province of [[Jambi]] and [[Penang]] Island (''Pulau Pinang'') off the west coast of [[Peninsular Malaysia]]. [[Fua Mulaku]] in the Maldives, [[Guwahati]] in [[Assam]], Supari (সুপারি) in [[West Bengal]] and coastal areas of [[Kerala]] and [[Karnataka]] in India, are also some of the places named after a local name for areca nut.{{citation needed|date=May 2023}}
